title: Finding DoRI: Discovery of Retained Images in Diffusion Models
claim: Mitigation that appears to remove memorized outputs is fragile: small adversarial perturbations still steer generation back to the memorized content.
layout: 2 panels split by dashed line; left image flow, right trajectory curves
description: The figure has two halves separated by a vertical dashed gray line. On the left, a training portrait photo feeds into a numbered flow: (1) a no-mitigation generation that replicates it. An arrow splits to two green-boxed generations labeled NeMo and Wanda (2, Mitigation), whose outputs differ visibly from the original. A blue fish icon (the adversarial embedding) then leads to two pink-boxed generations (3, Mitigation + Adv. Embedding) that again look like the training image. On the right, a noise square labeled Initial Noise sends curved arrows toward portraits. Three solid red/blue arrows (Adversarial Embeddings, Memorized Embedding) reach Data Replication. A dashed blue arrow, Memorized Embedding After Mitigation, ends at a different Mitigated Replication image. Green, pink, red and blue provide the contrast.
caption: Left: \scalebox{0.85}{\encircle{1}} Without mitigation, the DM closely replicates the training sample. \scalebox{0.85}{\encircle{2}} Mitigation strategies, such as pruning memorization weights with \nemo [ref] or \wanda [ref], prevent replication for the memorized prompt, thereby suggesting successful removal. Yet, \scalebox{0.85}{\encircle{3}} adversarial embeddings \img{figures/dory.png} still trigger replication. Right: While pruning alters the generation trajectory for the original memorized prompt (blue), adversarial embeddings steer denoising along alternative paths (red) that still lead to the memorized content, unaffected by the pruning-based mitigation.
abstract: Text-to-image diffusion models (DMs) have achieved remarkable success in image generation. However, concerns about data privacy and intellectual property remain due to their potential to inadvertently memorize and replicate training data. Recent mitigation efforts have focused on identifying and pruning weights responsible for triggering verbatim training data replication, based on the assumption that memorization can be localized. We challenge this assumption and demonstrate that, even after such pruning, small perturbations to the text embeddings of previously mitigated prompts can re-trigger data replication, revealing the fragility of such methods. Our further analysis then provides multiple indications that memorization is indeed \textit{not} inherently local: (1) replication triggers for memorized images are distributed throughout text embedding space; (2) embeddings yielding the same replicated image produce divergent model activations; and (3) different pruning methods identify inconsistent sets of memorization-related weights for the same image. Finally, we show that bypassing the locality assumption enables more robust mitigation through adversarial fine-tuning. These findings provide new insights into the fundamental nature of memorization in text-to-image DMs and inform the future development of more reliable mitigation methods against DM memorization.
